solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: More than one flower is found among rocky cairns (8)

indicators.note: 'found among' means sitting in the middle of something, so IS goes inside the other letters
rocky means unsteady and wobbling, so the letters of CAIRNS will not stay in their order

blocks.note: CAIRNS rearranged, split around the insert
used as itself, placed after NARC

annotation.surface: A walker spots a daffodil growing between the stones of a rugged cairn.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface uses 'is' as a plain verb, which hides that it supplies two letters. Flowers growing among hillside cairns makes the scene fit the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plural: narcissus is a flower genus including daffodils, and this is its Latin-style plural.

entries.clue: Note European confusion about one source of retribution from Greece (7)

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the word for confusion is wrapped around the one

blocks.note: N = note
E = European
a mess = confusion; it goes around the next piece
I = one, the Roman numeral, placed between MES and S

annotation.surface: A muddled European diplomatic note provokes some Greek revenge.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition names a figure from Greek myth: the goddess who punished human arrogance, whose name is now a common noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by origin: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution, and her name now means any agent of just punishment.

entries.clue: I will avoid disaster in series of performances (3)

indicators.note: to avoid something is to stay out of its way, so the I stays out of the word

blocks.note: the letter I, which must be removed
RUIN = disaster; the I between U and N is taken out

annotation.surface: An actor hopes to avoid a flop during a theatre season.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a nervous performer; the 'I' is not a speaker at all but a letter to be removed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain theatre sense: the stretch of consecutive performances a show gets is called its run.

entries.clue: Irrational behaviour keeping a river polluted? (10)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the irrational behaviour holds A and R inside

blocks.note: insanity = irrational behaviour; it opens up before its final Y
used as itself
R = river, standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether it is madness to let a river be polluted.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'polluted' is a loose, example-style definition: something polluted is one kind of unhealthy place.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: insanitary means dirty enough to endanger health, which pollution makes a place.

entries.clue: Newspaper arranged to entertain ambassador (5)

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them in your home, so one word takes the other inside

blocks.note: set = arranged, as in 'set the table'
HE = His Excellency, an ambassador's title; placed after S

annotation.surface: A newspaper organises a dinner to host a visiting ambassador.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' looks like an anagram indicator, but it is simply the word SET. An ambassador is addressed as His Excellency.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal term: a newspaper, especially a downmarket one, is called a sheet or a rag.

entries.clue: Surprise journey at an end (4,2)

blocks.note: a trip = a journey
'time's up' = time is at an end

annotation.surface: A traveller is caught off guard when the journey finishes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Surprise' reads as a noun but is a verb here, as in catching a witness off guard.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb sense: to catch someone out with something unexpected, as a cross-examiner does.

entries.clue: Water damage — care to drop initial temperature? (4)

indicators.note: an initial is a word's first letter, and dropping it means leaving it off

blocks.note: trust = care, as in 'left in my trust'
T = temperature, the first letter, which goes

annotation.surface: Someone recovering from a flood wonders whether to be less careful about the heating at first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initial temperature' reads like a thermostat setting, but it names the letter to lose: the T at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A cause-and-effect definition: the corrosion iron suffers when water and air get at it.

entries.clue: I only appear to move, though I may be given a roll (6,5)

definitions.text: though I may be given a roll

indicators.note: moving letters shifts them out of their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: An actor admits they only seem to move, yet may still be given a role.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the instrument: its keys seem to move by themselves, and a 'roll' here is the perforated paper roll that drives it, not a stage role.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: this self-playing instrument is fed a perforated paper roll that works its keys, though it may have no player.

entries.clue: Quietly stay asleep, say, in northern city (7)

blocks.note: P = piano, quietly in music
to rest on = to go on resting; sleeping is one example, hence 'say'

annotation.surface: A visitor to a northern city decides to have a quiet lie-in.
annotation.walkthrough: Preston is a city in Lancashire, in north-west England.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Preston is the city in Lancashire, north-west England.

entries.clue: Leave daughter in reception, up where air passengers sit? (8)

indicators.note: 'in' places the daughter's letter inside the reception word
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the word runs backward

blocks.note: go = leave
a salon = a reception room; turned upward it is NOLAS
D = daughter, placed after the first N

annotation.surface: A father leaving his daughter at a party asks where people will sit upstairs.
annotation.walkthrough: Gondolas suggest Venice, but the question mark hedges toward the passenger car of a balloon, airship or cable car.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the gondola is the cabin slung beneath a balloon, airship or cable car, where passengers ride.

entries.clue: Politician excited by trite manifestos (8,2,5)

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: A politician gets worked up about clichéd party manifestos.
annotation.walkthrough: In the UK a minister of state is a middle-ranking government minister, below a secretary of state.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this middle-ranking UK government post is held by an elected politician.

entries.clue: Marine movement bound to change when ebbing (6,4)

indicators.note: the tide ebbs by flowing back, so the word flows backward

blocks.note: a bound = a leap
to edit = to change; ebbing, it runs the other way

annotation.surface: Sea currents are sure to shift once the water goes out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bound to change' reads as 'certain to change', but bound is a leap. The answer has nothing to do with the season.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the extra-high and extra-low tides near new and full moon are a movement of the sea.

entries.clue: A cut in childcare disturbed those leading Irish children’s movement in the 1970s (7,4)

indicators.note: a cut word is trimmed short, losing its last letter
disturbed things are thrown out of order, so all the letters are mixed
the ones leading a line are at its front, so take the first letters

blocks.note: used as itself
CHILDCARE cut, losing its final E
the leading letters of Irish and children's

annotation.surface: Budget cuts to childcare upset Irish families, recalling a children's movement of the 1970s.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A cut in childcare' reads as a spending cut; really A sits beside a trimmed word. Tom Wolfe coined the phrase in 1970 to mock rich socialites taking up radical causes.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose label: the fashion among wealthy liberals for radical politics, named by Tom Wolfe in 1970, is called a movement here.

entries.clue: Hide offended feeling, welcoming learner (4)

indicators.note: welcoming someone means letting them in, so the learner goes inside

blocks.note: in a pet = in a sulk, a fit of offended feeling
L = learner, from L-plates; placed after PE

annotation.surface: Someone conceals their hurt feelings while still greeting a newcomer kindly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: an animal's skin. PET for a sulk is a dated British usage.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: an animal's skin with the fur on.

entries.clue: Limits to steady movement of sun and moon around year amounting to the same thing? (10)

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its boundaries, its first and last letters
movement shifts things about, so the letters change places
'around' means surrounding, so the mixed letters surround the year

blocks.note: limits of STEADY: its first and last letters
anagram fodder, rearranged and split around the year
Y = year

annotation.surface: An astronomer notes the steady cycles of sun and moon over a year come to much the same.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' here is just joining sun to moon for the anagram. The question mark flags a stretched definition: words that mean the same amount to the same thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose paraphrase: synonymous means having the same meaning, or so closely linked as to be equivalent.

entries.clue: Kept calm on bench, perhaps, following duke’s interruption (7)

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into something, so the duke's letter breaks into the word

blocks.note: sitting on a bench is one example of being seated
D = duke, inserted after SE

annotation.surface: A magistrate stayed composed on the bench after a duke burst in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On bench' suggests a court, but it just means sitting down. 'Following' is a link: the answer follows from the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical sense: a sedated patient has been kept calm with a drug.

entries.clue: Detail of the French copy superior to English (8)

indicators.note: superior literally means higher up, and in a down entry higher means earlier

blocks.note: des = French for 'of the' before a plural
to crib = to copy
E = English, placed below

annotation.surface: A detail from the French copy is judged better than the English one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Superior' reads as 'better', but in a down entry it means placed above. 'Detail' is a verb here.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to detail something is to set it out item by item.

entries.clue: Reveal love captured by song writer (3,4)

indicators.note: a captive is held inside, so love's letter is held within the other words

blocks.note: a lay = a song or ballad
O = love, zero in tennis
a pen writes

annotation.surface: A songwriter reveals that love has captured them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Song writer' looks like one word, songwriter, but it is two separate pieces with love between them.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal synonym: to lay something open is to expose it to view.

entries.clue: Notes enthusiastic comment when tucking into wines (7)

indicators.note: tucking into food puts it inside you, so the comment goes inside the wines

blocks.note: reds = red wines
cor! is a British exclamation of excitement

annotation.surface: A wine taster jots down excited remarks while sampling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notes' is a verb here, not the noun. 'Cor!' is British slang for 'wow!'.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to note something is to write it down or register it.

entries.clue: Volume is evident in rising row? Consider again (7)

indicators.note: something evident in a thing can be seen within it, so these letters sit inside
in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom up

blocks.note: a tier = a row; rising, it runs backward
V = volume
used as itself; V and IS sit after RE

annotation.surface: A noise complaint asks whether a rowdy tier of spectators should be looked at again.
annotation.walkthrough: The row is a tier, as in stadium seating, not an argument, and 'volume' is not loudness but an abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: to revisit an idea is to go back to it and think it over.

entries.clue: Cat in bag: hard to tolerate (7)

indicators.note: 'in' puts the cat inside the bag

blocks.note: a tom = a male cat
a sac is a bag, as in the body
H = hard, as on pencils

annotation.surface: Letting the cat out of the bag is hard to put up with.
annotation.walkthrough: A cat in a bag calls up the idiom, but the cat is a tom and the bag is a sac.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative verb: to stomach something is to be able to digest it, so to put up with it.

entries.clue: Complete circuit in operation (4,3)

blocks.note: in = at home
a run = an operation, as in a production run

annotation.surface: An electrician confirms the wiring loop is finished and working.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is electrical, a closed circuit with current flowing; the answer is from baseball, where the batter circles all four bases.
annotation.definitionFit: A baseball sense: a hit that lets the batter run a full circuit of the bases in one go.

entries.clue: Poll closing early, restricting Liberal in potential measure (4)

indicators.note: something closing early stops before its end, so the last letter is lost
to restrict is to hem in, so the Liberal's letter is hemmed inside

blocks.note: VOTE = poll, closing early to lose the E
L = Liberal, placed after VO

annotation.surface: An early poll closure hampers the Liberals in a possible policy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Potential measure' looks political, but it is electrical: potential difference is what this unit measures.
annotation.definitionFit: A unit definition: this SI unit measures electric potential difference.

entries.clue: Left back hardly gutted to secure rotating space for awards (6,4)

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction, so the word reads backward
gutting removes the insides, leaving only the outer letters
a rotating thing turns around, so the word is turned end to end

blocks.note: port = left, on a ship; turned back
HARDLY emptied of its middle
to moor = to secure a boat; turned around

annotation.surface: A football left back, barely disappointed, wins a place in the club's trophy cabinet.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is football: a left back is a defender, and 'gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed. Port is the left side of a ship.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a room set aside for displaying trophies is a space for awards.

entries.clue: Receiver always under pressure before end of game (5)

indicators.note: in a down entry, under means placed below, so AYE comes after P
the end of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: P = pressure
aye = always, old poetic use as in 'for aye'
the last letter of GAME

annotation.surface: A wide receiver is always under pressure as the game closes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Receiver' suggests a phone or an American football player; here it is someone who receives money.
annotation.definitionFit: A financial sense: the person to whom a payment is made is its receiver.

entries.clue: Source of mildew following in place of mould (4)

indicators.note: the source of something is where it starts, so take the first letter
a follower comes behind, so M is placed after the other piece

blocks.note: 'for' can mean 'instead of', as in 'swap this for that'
the first letter of MILDEW

annotation.surface: A gardener finds mildew growing where mould once was.
annotation.walkthrough: Mildew and mould belong together in the surface, but 'mould' is the definition in its shaping sense, not the fungus.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to mould clay is to shape it.

entries.clue: Harry Potter and the Banshee? It’s basically wrong (9,6)

blocks.note: Harry Potter is a pupil at Hogwarts, a definition by example
a banshee is an Irish wailing spirit, another definition by example

annotation.surface: It reads like a new Harry Potter title, dismissed as fundamentally mistaken.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the charade are examples rather than synonyms, which is why the question mark is there. 'Basically' points to an elementary error.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: this is a glaring elementary mistake, the kind a pupil makes, so basically wrong.

entries.clue: Down, barely moving, with second kept away (3)

indicators.note: something kept away is not allowed in, so the letter is left out

blocks.note: slow = barely moving
S = second, the letter removed from the front

annotation.surface: Someone feeling down barely moves, with a helper kept away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' could be a helper in a duel or boxing, but it is only the abbreviation S.
annotation.definitionFit: A mood synonym: feeling low and feeling down both mean dispirited.

entries.clue: American city cheers The Big Sleep? (6)

blocks.note: ta = thanks, British informal, like cheers
a coma is a big, deep sleep

annotation.surface: Someone raises a glass to an American city and a classic noir film.
annotation.walkthrough: The Big Sleep is a Raymond Chandler novel and film, set in Los Angeles; here it is just a very deep sleep. 'Cheers' and 'ta' both mean thanks in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Tacoma is a port city in Washington state, USA.

entries.clue: Whingers upset American composer (8)

indicators.note: upsetting something knocks it over, so the letters tumble into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: Complainers annoy an American composer.
annotation.walkthrough: A whinger is British slang for a complainer.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: George Gershwin, who wrote Rhapsody in Blue, was an American composer.
